newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Oil stocks key to prices again next year.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Oil stocks key to prices again next year.

text.p: The oil industry is not likely to beef up inventories in 1997 now that Iraqi crude oil is in the pipeline and non-OPEC producers are gradually turning up the pumps, analysts say.

But these two factors should ensure that stocks return to more normal levels although the repeated draws of recent years and "just-in-time" refinery management should make for another year of volatile prices.

The depleted state of oil industry stocks, at historically low levels following the protracted cold winter of 1995, played a pivotal role in taking crude oil prices to just above $25 a barrel in October, the highest level since 1991.

But analysts say conditions which made for such tight fundamentals this year are unlikely to be repeated in 1997. Furthermore, an unseasonal stock build in the first quarter has not been ruled out, which could set a softer tone for prices for the rest of 1997.
"With Iraq coming back, the inventory situation should start to revert towards its normal level," said Gordon Gray, European energy analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.
He added that the seasonal drawdown in stocks was not expected to be as big as the same time last year.

Analysts say delayed maintenance in the United States, where some refineries pushed back turnarounds to cope with heating oil demand and beef up low inventories, will be bunched into January and prevent a huge draw in the first quarter of next year.

The rationale of last year's low stocks was based on the economics of a market where forward prices are lower than prompt and holding stocks would mean sitting on depreciating assets and using up operating capital.

The strategy could change if additional supply weakened the market to the extent that it would slip into contango -- where forward prices are higher than prompt --- and make stock-building a more economic option.

The industry will be starting 1997 with a low stock base but there are signs from U.S.data of a gradual build in middle distillates and gasoline stocks, which will hold the key to next year's price structure.

The IEA said in its latest Monthly Oil Market Report that U.S. refining maintenance shutdowns in the U.S. Gulf region were expected to "increase above normal levels in early 1997." It said the extent of the shutdowns would be influenced by gas oil and gasoline inventories.
The weather is key in determining whether refineries have to keep pushing out middle distillates production at the expense of gasoline, which will take the driving seat come the spring quarter.

"Gasoline looks like the unignited fire of the market," said Russ Hill, senior oil trader in London for Austrian oil company OMV. "With turnarounds expected early next year, read that we are headed for a 25-year low in gasoline stocks, we could go ballistic."
"Iraq is of no real issue at the moment, but it could become an issue as we get into the fourth or fifth month of delivery at a time when turnarounds are significant," Hill said.
Mari Buglass, analyst at Smith Barney, believes the industry will not see any incentive to build stocks in a backwardated market.
"Has the industry learned its lesson? Will they build in the second and third quarters? Even if they wanted to, their accountants wouldn't let them," she said.

The IEA anticipates demand for OPEC crude and stocks in the first quarter of 1997 at 26.5 million barrels per day (bpd). It sees current OPEC production at 26.14 million bpd against an agreed ceiling of 25.03 million/
Assuming there was no increase and that Iraq was still out of the market, although its share of exports is factored into the OPEC ceiling, this would translate into a stock draw of 400,000 bpd.
With Iraq expected to pump 650,000 bpd a month for six months under the U.N. "oil-for-food" deal while non-OPEC supply is forecast to surge, the industry could in fact see a stock build.
Kleinwort Benson Research in their latest World Oil Report project a 1997 stock build of 500,000 bpd, which they said was what the market will need given the repeated draws of recent years.
"Certainly, another year of zero build or even a draw would leave the market dangerously exposed to oil price volatility next year, especially on the upside," the report said.

"The chances of a stock build next year probably outweigh the risk of another draw. The key reason behind our view is that another year of inventory draw would imply a cut in OPEC production which should be dismissed as a possibility for all practical purposes," it added.
